entries.ea4e54395de1bafdea8aaf297cca0f19d6b6fa4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9204"/><div sID="gen15686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9204"/><hi type="bold">17. in the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Is 45:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.25">25</reference>), contrasted with the idols which cannot give even temporary help (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Is 45:16</reference>); in Jehovah there is everlasting salvation (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Is 26:4</reference>).<div eID="gen15686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... ashamed--</hi>opposed to the doom of the idolaters, who, in the hour of need, shall be "ashamed" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Is 45:16</reference>). <div eID="gen15687" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e63bce4866fabb697112d0d25f876282764c470: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9205"/><div sID="gen15688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9205"/>18. (See on <reference osisRef="Isa.45.12">Is 45:12</reference>).<div eID="gen15688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited--</hi>Therefore, Judah, lying waste during the Babylonish captivity, shall be peopled again by the exiles. The Jews, from this passage, infer that, after the resurrection, the earth shall be inhabited, for there can be no reason why the earth should then exist in vain any more than now (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:13</reference>). <div eID="gen15689" type="x-p"/>
entries.81ed533c87ecceac58c4791334a4c3b25e49a460: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9206"/><div sID="gen15690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9206"/><hi type="bold">19. not ... secret--</hi>not like the heathen oracles which gave their responses from dark caverns, with studied obscurity (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Is 48:16</reference>). Christ plainly quotes these words, thereby identifying Himself with Jehovah (<reference osisRef="John.18.20">Joh 18:20</reference>).<div eID="gen15690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I said not ... Seek ... in vain--</hi>When I commanded you to seek Me (Jehovah did so, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.11">Is 45:11</reference>, "Ask Me," &c.), it was not in order that ye might be sent empty away (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.47">De 32:47</reference>). Especially in Israel's time of trial, God's interposition, in behalf of Zion hereafter, is expressly stated as about to be the answer to prayer (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7-Isa.62.10">7-10</reference>; Psa 102:13-17, 19-21). So in the case of all believers, the spiritual Israel.<div eID="gen15691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>that which is veracious: not in the equivocal terms of heathen responses, fitly symbolized by the "dark places" from which they were uttered.<div eID="gen15692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right--</hi>true (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Is 41:26</reference>). <div eID="gen15693" type="x-p"/>
entries.33422eb7af692e70e4c2328ab09977b1b9e173b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9207"/><div sID="gen15694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9207"/><hi type="bold">20. escaped of the nations--</hi>those of the nations who shall have escaped the slaughter inflicted by Cyrus. Now, at last, ye shall see the folly of "praying to a god that cannot save" (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Is 45:16</reference>). Ultimately, those that shall be "left of all the nations which shall come against Jerusalem" are meant (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). They shall then all be converted to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Is 66:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.20-Zech.8.23">Zec 8:20-23</reference>). <div eID="gen15694" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a19fba0965bc9afbb010cc1aeef8b3a26376b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9208"/><div sID="gen15695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9208"/>21. Challenge the worshippers of idols (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Is 41:1</reference>).<div eID="gen15695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take counsel together--</hi>as to the best arguments wherewith to defend the cause of idolatry.<div eID="gen15696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who ... from that time--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.22">Is 41:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">23</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Is 44:8</reference>). Which of the idols has done what God hath, namely, foretold, primarily as to Cyrus; ultimately as to the final restoration of Israel hereafter? The idolatry of Israel before Cyrus' time will have its counterpart in the Antichrist and the apostasy, which shall precede Christ's manifestation.<div eID="gen15697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">just ... and ... Saviour--</hi>righteous in keeping His promises, and therefore a Saviour to His people. Not only is it not inconsistent with, but it is the result of, His righteousness, or justice, that He should save His redeemed (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.6">Is 42:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.10">Psa 85:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">Ro 3:26</reference>). <div eID="gen15698" type="x-p"/>
entries.342cda4c9366ceec1cad5400fe037e2b0cf7a31e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9209"/><div sID="gen15699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9209"/><hi type="bold">22. Look ... and be ye saved--</hi>The second imperative expresses the result which will follow obedience to the first (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.18">Ge 42:18</reference>); ye shall be saved (<reference osisRef="John.3.14">Joh 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.15">15</reference>). <reference osisRef="Num.21.9">Nu 21:9</reference>: "If a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass he lived." What so simple as a look? Not do something, but look to the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.30">Ac 16:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.31">31</reference>). Believers look by faith, the eye of the soul. The look is that of one turning (see Margin) to God, as at once "Just and the Saviour" (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>), that is, the look of conversion (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">Psa 22:27</reference>). <div eID="gen15699" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5b32853ed916c5799fbbad3d7c6699fec05a6f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9210"/><div sID="gen15700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9210"/><hi type="bold">23. sworn by myself--</hi>equivalent to, "As I live," as <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Ro 14:11</reference> quotes it. So <reference osisRef="Num.14.21">Nu 14:21</reference>. God could swear by no greater, therefore He swears by Himself (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.13">He 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen15700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word ... in righteousness--</hi>rather, "the truth (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>) is gone forth from My mouth, the word (of promise), and it shall not return (that is, which shall not be revoked)" [Lowth]. But the accents favor English Version.<div eID="gen15701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongue ... swear--</hi>namely, an oath of allegiance to God as their true King (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Is 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">Is 65:16</reference>). Yet to be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>). <div eID="gen15702" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b3391854c6e79c7321c59c960cb7b1a8532b1c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9211"/><div sID="gen15703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9211"/>24. Rather, "Only in Jehovah shall men say of me (this clause is parenthetical), is there righteousness" (which includes salvation, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>, "a just God and a Saviour," <reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">Is 46:13</reference>), &c. [Maurer].<div eID="gen15703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>namely, to save.<div eID="gen15704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall men come--</hi>Those who have set themselves up against God shall come to Him in penitence for the past (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.22">Is 19:22</reference>).<div eID="gen15705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ashamed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Is 45:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">Is 54:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.11">41:11</reference>). <div eID="gen15706" type="x-p"/>
entries.28fb85b3c68ed61527526c3adc2e1f80d77ac3fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9212"/><div sID="gen15707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9212"/><hi type="bold">25. all ... Israel--</hi>the spiritual Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Ro 2:29</reference>) and the literal Israel, that is, the final remnant which shall all be saved (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.17">Is 45:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>).<div eID="gen15707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justified--</hi>treated as if they were just, through Christ's righteousness and death (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen15708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>literally, "sing" in His praise (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.24">Jr 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">1Co 1:31</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.45"/>

entries.11b19ff2412daf9a4efff49a6c5a5fcb42845a7f: <div eID="gen28300" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> Prophecy concerning Cyrus, the first king of the Persians. Every obstruction shall be removed out of his way, and the treasures taken from his enemies shall be immense, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.3">Isa 45:1-3</reference>, To whom, and on what account, Cyrus was indebted for his wonderful success, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4-Isa.45.6">Isa 45:4-6</reference>. The prophet refutes the absurd opinion of the Persians, that there were two supreme beings, an evil and a good one, represented by light and darkness, here declared to be only the operation of the One true God, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.7">Isa 45:7</reference>; and makes a transition to the still greater work of God displayed in the dispensation of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>. Great impiety of those who call in question the mysterious providence of God towards his children, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9-Isa.45.12">Isa 45:9-12</reference>. The remaining part of this chapter, interspersed with strictures on the absurdity of idolatry and some allusions to the dark lying oracles of the heathens, may partly refer to the deliverance begun by Cyrus, but chiefly to the salvation by the Messiah, which, it is declared, shall be of universal extent and everlasting duration, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.13-Isa.45.25">Isa 45:13-25</reference>. <div eID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> Loose the loins of kings "ungird the loins of kings" - See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Isa 5:27</reference>. Xenophon gives the following list of the nations conquered by Cyrus: the Syrians, Assyrians, Arabians, Cappadocians, both the Phrygians, Lydians, Carians, Phoenicians, Babylonians. He moreover reigned over the Bactrians, Indians, Cilicians, the Sacae Paphlagones, and ldariandyni. - Cyrop., lib. 1 p. 4, Edit. Hutchinson, Quarto. All these kingdoms he acknowledges, in his decree for the restoration of the Jews, to have been given to him by Jehovah, the God of heaven. <reference osisRef="Ezr.1.2">Ezr 1:2</reference>. <div eID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> To open before him the two leaved gates, etc. "That I may open before him the valves; and the gates shall not be shut" - The gates of Babylon within the city leading from the streets to the river, were providentially left open, when Cyrus's forces entered the city in the night through the channel of the river, in the general disorder occasioned by the great feast which was then celebrated; otherwise, says Herodotus, 1:191, the Persians would have been shut up in the bed of the river, and taken as in a net, and all destroyed. And the gates of the palace were opened imprudently by the king's orders, to inquire what was the cause of the tumult without; when the two parties under Gobrias and Gadatas rushed in, got possession of the palace, and slew the king. - Xenoph., Cyrop. 7 p. 528.
entries.d6d123a28a2320cd458d577ff72e56709f0eab29: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> The crooked places "The mountains" - For הדורים hodurim, crooked places, a word not easily accounted for in this place, the Septuagint read הררים hararim, τα ορη, the mountains. Two MSS. have הדרים hadarim, without the ו vau, which is hardly distinguishable from the reading of the Septuagint. The Divine protection that attended Cyrus, and rendered his expedition against Babylon easy and prosperous is finely expressed by God's going before him, and making the mountains level. The image is highly poetical: - <div eID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> At vos, qua veniet, tumidi subsidite montes, <div eID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> Et faciles curvis vallibus este viae. <div eID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> Ovid, Amor. 2:16. "Let the lofty mountains fall down, and make level paths in the crooked valleys." <div eID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> The gates of brass "The valves of brass" - Abydenus, apud, Euseb. Praep. Evang. 9:41, says, that the wall of Babylon had brazen gates. And Herodotus, i, 179. more particularly: "In the wall all round there are a hundred gates, all of brass; and so in like manner are the sides and the lintels." The gates likewise within the city, opening to the river from the several streets, were of brass; as were those also of the temple of Belus. - Herod. i., 180, 181.
entries.e76db3853bf4f7f584c52d5a4e930978afd83e19: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> I will gave thee the treasures of darkness - Sardes and Babylon, when taken by Cyrus, were the wealthiest cities in the world. Croesus, celebrated beyond all the kings of that age for his riches, gave up his treasures to Cyrus, with an exact account in writing of the whole, containing the particulars with which each wagon was loaded when they were carried away; and they were delivered to Cyrus at the palace of Babylon. - Xenoph. Cyrop. lib. 7 p. 503, 515, 540. <div eID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> Pliny gives the following account of the wealth taken by Cyrus in Asia. Jam Cyrus devicta Asia, pondo 34 millia auri invenerat; praeter vasa aurea, aurumque factum, et in eo folia, ac platanum, vitemque. Qua victoria argenti quingenta millia talentorum reportavit; et craterem Semiramidis, cuius pondus quindecim talents colligebat. Talentum autem Aegyptium pondo lxxx. patere 50 capere Varro tradit. - Nat. Hist. 33:15. "When Cyrus conquered Asia, he found thirty-four thousand pounds weight of gold, besides golden vessels and articles in gold; and leaves, (folia, perhaps solia, bathing vessels, Hol.), a plane, and vine tree, (of gold.) By which victory he carried away fifteen thousand talents of silver; and the cup of Semiramis, the weight of which was fifteen tatents. The Egyptian talent, according to Varro, was eighty pounds." This cup was the crater, or large vessel, out of which they filled the drinking cups at great entertainments. Evidently it could not be a drinking vessel, which, according to what Varro and Pliny say, must have weighed 1, 200 pounds! <div eID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> The gold and silver estimated by weight in this account, being converted into pounds sterling, amount to one hundred and twenty-six millions two hwndred and twenty-four thousand pounds. - Brerewood, De Ponderibus, cap. x. <div eID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> Treasures of darkness may refer to the custom of burying their jewels and money under the ground in their house floors, fearing robbers.
entries.7bed58ea1127f3548768b1c49b466d59bbe9ef05: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> I form the light, and create darkness - It was the great principle of the Magian religion, which prevailed in Persia in the time of Cyrus, and in which probably he was educated, that there are two supreme, co-eternal, and independent causes always acting in opposition one to the other; one the author of all good, the other of all evil. The good being they called Light; the evil being, Darkness. That when Light had the ascendant, then good and happtness prevailed among men; when Darkness had the superiority, then eviI and misery abounded. An opinion that contradicts the clearest evidence of our reason, which plainly leads us to the acknowledgment of one only Supreme Being, infinitely good as well as powerful. With reference to this absurd opinion, held by the person to whom this prophecy is addressed, God, by his prophet, in the most significant terms, asserts his omnipotence and absolute supremacy: - "I am Jehovah, and none else; <div eID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> Forming light, and creating darkness, <div eID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> Making peace, and creating evil: <div eID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> I Jehovah am the author of all these things." <div eID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> Declaring that those powers whom the Persians held to be the original authors of good and evil to mankind, representing them by light and darkness, as their proper emblems, are no other than creatures of God, the instruments which he employs in his government of the world, ordained or permitted by him in order to execute his wise and just decrees; and that there is no power, either of good or evil, independent of the one supreme God, infinite in power and in goodness. <div eID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> There were, however, some among the Persians whose sentiments were more moderate as to this matter; who held the evil principle to be in some measure subordinate to the good; and that the former would at length be wholly subdued by the latter. See Hyde, De Relig. Vet. Pers. cap. xxii. <div eID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> That this opinion prevailed among the Persians as early as the time of Cyrus we may, I think, infer not only from this passage of Isaiah, which has a manifest reference to it, but likewise from a passage in Xenophon's Cyropaedia, where the same doctrine is applied to the human mind. Araspes, a noble young Persian, had fallen in love with the fair captive Panthea, committed to his charge by Cyrus. After all his boasting that he was superior to the assaults of that passion, he yielded so far to it as even to threaten violence if she would not comply with his desires. Awed by the reproof of Cyrus, fearing his displeasure, and having by cool reflection recovered his reason; in his discourse with him on this subject he says: "O Cyrus, I have certainly two souls; alld this piece of philosophy I have learned from that wicked sophist, Love. For if I had but one soul, it would not be at the same time good and evil, it would not at the same time approve of honorable and base actions; and at once desire to do, and refuse to do, the very same things. But it is plain that I am animated by two souls, and when the good soul prevails, I do what is virtuous; and when the evil one prevails, I attempt what is vicious. But now the good soul prevails, having gotten you for her assistant, and has clearly gained the superiority." Lib. 6 p. 424. <div eID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> I make peace, and create evil - Evil is here evidently put for war and its attendant miseries. I will procure peace for the Israelites, and destroy Babylon by war. I form light, and create darkness. Now, as darkness is only the privation of light, so the evil of war is the privation of peace.
entries.a758bfd84c57564715536b74a27d3d784ac43f09: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> Drop down, ye heavens - The eighty-fifth psalm is a very elegant ode on the same subject with this part of Isaiah's prophecies, the restoration of Judah from captivity; and is, in the most beautiful part of it, a manifest imitation of this passage of the prophet: - "Verily his salvation is nigh unto them that fear him, <div eID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> That glory may dwell in our land. <div eID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> Mercy and truth have met together; <div eID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> Righteousness and peace have kissed each other. <div eID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> Truth shall spring from the earth, <div eID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> And righteousness shall look down from heaven. <div eID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> Even Jehovah: will give that which is good, <div eID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> And our land shall yield her produce. <div eID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> Righteousness shall go before him, <div eID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> And shall direct his footsteps in the way." <div eID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> Psalm 85:10-14. <div eID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> See the notes on these verses. <div eID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> These images of the dew and the rain descending from heaven and making the earth fruitful, employed by the prophet, and some of those nearly of the same kind which are used by the psalmist, may perhaps be primarily understood as designed to set forth in a splendid manner the happy state of God's people restored to their country, and flourishing in peace and plenty, in piety and virtue; but justice and salvation, mercy and truth, righteousness and peace, and glory dwelling in the land, cannot with any sort of propriety, in the one or the other, be interpreted as the consequences of that event; they must mean the blessings of the great redemption by Messiah. <div eID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> Let the earth open, etc. - Jonathan, in his Targum, refers this to the resurrection of the dead; the earth shall be opened, ויחון מיתיא veyechon meiteiya, and the dead shall revive. A plain proof that the ancient Jews believed in a future state, and acknowledged the resurrection of the dead. <div eID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> Let them bring forth salvation "Let salvation produce her fruit" - For ויפרו vaiyiphru, the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac read ויפרה vaiyiphrah; and one MS. has a rasure close after the latter ו vau, which probably was ה he at first.
entries.93af3a5b841eae0fd1185d4592c64b06980ef3a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> Wo unto him that striveth with his Maker "To unto him that contendeth with the power that formed him" - The prophet answers or prevents the objections and cavils of the unbelieving Jews, disposed to murmur against God, and to arraign the wisdom and justice of his dispensations in regard to them; in permitting them to be oppressed by their enemies, and in promising them deliverance instead of preventing their captivity. St. Paul has borrowed the image, and has applied it to the like purpose with equal force and elegance: "Nay, but, O man! who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, out of the same lump to make one vessel to honor, and another to dishonor?" <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Rom 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">Rom 9:21</reference>. This is spoken says Kimchi, against the king of Babylon, who insulted the Most High, bringing forth the sacred vessels, drinking out of them, and magnifying himself against God. <div eID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> Or thy work, He hath no hands "And to the workman, Thou hast no hands" - The Syriac renders, as if he had read, ולא היתי פעל ידיך velo hayithi pheal yadeycha, "neither am I the work of thy hands;" the Septuagint, as if they had reads ולא פעלת ואין ודים לך velo phaalta veeyn yaadim lecha, "neither hast thou made me; and thou hast no hands." But the fault seems to be in the transposition of the two pronouns; for ופעלך uphoolcha, read ופעלו uphoolo: and for לו lo, read לך lecha. So Houbigant corrects it; reading also ופעלו uphoolo; which last correction seems not altogether necessary. The Septuagint, in MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2 have it thus, και το εργον ουκ εχεις χειρας, which favors the reading here proposed.
entries.39885230c4601c9049322e2d56b21652c0b94f36: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> Ask me of things to come "And he that formeth the things which are to come" - I read ויוצר veyotser, without the ו vau suffixed; from the Septuagint, who join it in construction with the following word, ὁ ποιησας τα επερχομενα. "Do ye question me." - תשאלוני tishaluni, Chald. recte; praecedit ת tau; et sic forte legerunt reliqui Intt. - Secker. "The Chaldee has, more properly, תשאלוני tishaluni, with a ת tau preceding; and thus the other interpreters probably read." The learned bishop therefore reads the passage thus: - "Thus saith Jehovah, the Holy One of Israel; <div eID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> And he that formeth the things which are to come; <div eID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> Do ye question me concerning my children? <div eID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> And do ye give me directions concerning the work of my hands?"
entries.415b0f942d560d97d6d17c9d1c8886edfa39031c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> I have raised him up - This evidently refers to Cyrus, and to what he did for the Jews; and informs us by whom he was excited to do it.
entries.f15d37a1a55ab268b498947ec4ceb3ac9e3a92f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> The labor of Egypt "The wealth of Egypt" - This seems to relate to the future admission of the Gentiles into the Church of God. Compare <reference osisRef="Psa.68.32">Psa 68:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.72.10">Psa 72:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.60.6-Psa.60.9">Psa 60:6-9</reference>. And perhaps these particular nations may be named, by a metonymy common in all poetry, for powerful and wealthy nations in general. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Isa 60:1</reference>. <div eID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> The Sabeans, men of stature "The Sabeans, tall of stature" - That the Sabeans were of a more majestic appearance than common, is particularly remarked by Agatharchides, an ancient Greek historian quoted by Bochart, Phaleg, 2:26, τα σωματα εστι των κατοικουντων αξιολογωτερα. So also the Septuagint understand it, rendering it ανδρες ὑψηλοι, "tall men." And the same phrase, אנשי מדה anshey middah, is used for persons of extraordinary stature, <reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Num 13:32</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6">1Chr 20:6</reference>. <div eID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> They shall make supplication unto thee "They shall in suppliant guise address thee" - The conjunction ו vau is supplied by the ancient Versions, and confirmed by fifteen MSS. of Kennicott's, (seven ancient), thirteen of De Rossi's, and six editions, ואליך veelayich. Three MSS. (two ancient) omit the ו vau before אליך elaylch at the beginning of the line.
entries.40aca4da0749d5605f8ac3e1ec78d7020c1a4041: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself - At present, from the nations of the world. <div eID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> O God of Israel, the Savior - While thou revealest thyself to the Israelites and savest them.
entries.a612ed58de1ea552e423a3a7314b7e00957b449f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> They shall be ashamed "They are ashamed" - The reader cannot but observe the sudden transition from the solemn adoration of the secret and mysterious nature of God's counsels in regard to his people, to the spirited denunciation of the confusion of idolaters, and the final destruction of idolatry; contrasted with the salvation of Israel, not from temporal captivity, but the eternal salvation by the Messiah, strongly marked by the repetition and augmentation of the phrase, to the ages of eternity. But there is not only a sudden change in the sentiment, the change is equally observable in the construction of the sentences; which from the usual short measure, runs out at once into two distichs of the longer sort of verse. See Prelim. Dissert. p. 66, etc. There is another instance of the same kind and very like to this, of a sudden transition in regard both to the sentiment and construction in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.17">Isa 42:17</reference>. "His adversaries" - This line, to the great diminution of the beauty of the distich, is imperfect in the present text: the subject of the proposition is not particularly expressed, as it is in the line following. The version of the Septuagint happily supplies the word that is lost: οἱ αντικειμενοι αυτῳ, "his adversaries," the original word was צריו tsaraiv. - L.
entries.6c8479da85171289b37c9c5e448b867cb4ae0bae: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> He formed it to be inhabited "For he formed it to be inhabited" - An ancient MS. has כי ki before לשבת lashebeth; and so the ancient Versions.
entries.8ffa4fed6de38cdc59ac4df20fad87efd52c3d2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> I have not spoken tn secret, in a dark place of the earth - In opposition to the manner in which the heathen oracles gave their answers, which were generally delivered from some deep and obscure cavern. Such was the seat of the Cumean Sybil: - <div eID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> Excisum Euboicae latus ingens rupis in antrum. <div eID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> Virg. Aen. 6:42. "A cave cut in the side of a huge rock." <div eID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> Such was that of the famous oracle at Delphi; of which, says Strabo, lib. ix., φασι δ' ειναι το μαντειον αντρον κοιλον μετα βαθους, ου μαλα ευρυστομον. "The oracle is said to be a hollow cavern of considerable depth, with an opening not very wide." And Diodorus, giving an account of the origin of this oracle, says "that there was in that place a great chasm or cleft in the earth; in which very place is now situated what is called the Adytum of the temple." Αδυτον· σπηλαιον, η το αποκρυφον μερος του ἱερου. Mesych. "Adytum means a cavern, or the hidden part of the temple." <div eID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> I the Lord speak righteousness, I declare things that are right "I am Jehovah, who speak truth, who give direct answers" - This also is said in opposition to the false and ambiguous answers given by the heathen oracles, of which there are many noted examples; none more so than that of the answer given to Croesus when he marehed against Cyrus, which piece of history has some connection with this part of Isaiah's prophecies. Let us hear Cicero's account of the Delphic answers in general, and of this in particular: Sed jam ad te venio, <div eID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> O sancte Apollo, qui umbilicum certum terrarum obsides, <div eID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> Unde superstitiosa primum saeva evasit vox fera. <div eID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> Tuis enim oraculis Chrysippus totum volumen implevit, partim falsis, ut ego opinor; partim casu veris, ut fit in omni oratione saepissime; partim flexiloquis et obscuris, ut interpres egeat interprete, et sors ipsa ad sortes referenda sit; partim ambiguis, et quae ad dialecticum deferenda sint. Nam cum sors illa edita est opulentissimo regi Asiea, Croesus Halym penetrans magnam pervertet opum vim: hostium vim sese perversurum putavit; pervertit autem suam. Utrum igitur eorum accidisset, verum oraculum fuisset. De Divinat. 2:56. Mountainous countries, and those which abounded in chasms, caves, and grottos, were the places in which oracles were most frequent. The horror and gloom inspired by such places were useful to the lying priests in their system of deception. The terms in which those oracles were conceived, (they were always ambiguous, or equivocal, or false, or illusory), sometimes the turn of a phrase, or a peculiarity in idiom or construction which might be turned pro or con, contained the essence of the oracular declaration. Sometimes, in the multitude of guesses, one turned out to be true; at other times, so equivocal was the oracle, that, however the thing fell out, the declaration could be interpreted in that way, as in the above to Croesus, from the oracle at Delphi, which was: If Croeses march against Cyrus, he shall overthrow a great empire: he, supposing that this promised him success, fought, and lost his own, while he expected to destroy that of his enemy. Here the quack demon took refuge in his designed ambiguity. He predicted the destruction of a great empire, but did not say which it was; and therefore he was safe, howsoever the case fell out. Not one of the predictions of God's prophets is conceived in this way.
entries.41565e6816972d1f5af44e195b5627bba7fd7df3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> Bring them near; yea, let them take counsel together - For יועצו yoatsu or yivvaatsu, let them consult, the Septuagint read ידעו yedau, let them know. but an ancient MS. has יועדו yoedu, let them come together by appointment; which may probably be the true reading.
entries.e5c90e4d8358387409b44153f11708c995af9a5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> Look unto me, and be ye saved, etc. - This verse and the following contain a plain prediction of the universal spread of the knowledge of God through Christ; and so the Targum appears to have understood it; see <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Rom 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phi.2.10">Phi 2:10</reference>. The reading of the Targum is remarkable, viz., אתפנו למימרי ithpeno lemeymri, look to my Word, ὁ Λογος, the Lord Jesus.
entries.086c4a818bb0151023ff04d947793e476273f698: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> I have sworn by myself - במימרי bemeymri, by my Word: and the word - פתגם pithgam, or saying, to distinguish it from the personal substantial Word meymra, mentioned before. See the Targum. <div eID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> The word is gone out of my mouth "Truth is gone forth from my mouth; the word" - So the Septuagint distinguish the members of the sentence, preserving the elegance of the construction and the clearness of the sense.
entries.3a0837adfbd0b4b30394d31b629e51a15270b113: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> Surely, shall one say, In the Lord have I righteousness and strength "Saying, Only to Jehovah belongeth salvation and power" - A MS. omits לי li, unto me; and instead of לי אמר li amar, he said or shall say unto me, the Septuagint read, in the copy which they used, לאמר lemor, saying. For יבא yabo, He shall come, in the singular, twelve MSS. three ancient) read יבאו yabeu, plural; and a letter is erased at the end of the word in two others: and so the Alexandrine copy of the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read it. For צדקות tsedakoth plural, two MSS. read צדקת tsidkath, singular; and so the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee. <div eID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28366" type="x-p"/> Probably these are the words of Cyrus, who acknowledged that all his success came from Jehovah. And this sentiment is in effect contained in his decree or proclamation, <reference osisRef="Ezr.1.2">Ezr 1:2</reference> : "Thus saith Cyrus, king of Persia, The Lord God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth, "etc.  <chapter eID="Isa.45"/> <div eID="gen28366" type="x-p"/>

entries.2986238287e7da597cc3acd042c10432b11fbe08: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.3">Isa 45:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13420" type="x-p"/> The first strophe of the first half of this sixth prophecy (Isa 44:24.), the subject of which is Cyrus, the predicted restorer of Jerusalem, of the cities of Judah, and of the temple, is now followed by a second strophe (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.8">Isa 45:1-8</reference>), having for its subject Cyrus, the man through whose irresistible career of conquest the heathen would be brought to recognise the power of Jehovah, so that heavenly blessings would come down upon the earth. The naming of the great shepherd of the nations, and the address of him, are continued in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.3">Isa 45:1-3</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah to His anointed, to Koresh, whom I have taken by his right hand to subdue nations before him; and the loins of kings I ungird, to open before him doors and gates, that they may not continue shut. I shall go before thee, and level what is heaped up: gates of brass shall I break in pieces, and bolts of iron shall I smite to the ground. And I shall give thee treasures of darkness, and jewels of hidden places, that thou mayest know that I Jehovah am He who called out thy name, (even) the God of Israel.”</hi> The words addressed to Cyrus by Jehovah commence in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Isa 45:2</reference>, but promises applying to him force themselves into the introduction, being evoked by the mention of his name. He is the only king of the Gentiles whom Jehovah ever <hi type="italic">meshı̄chı̄</hi> (my anointed; lxx τῷ χριστῷ μου). The fundamental principle of the politics of the empire of the world was all-absorbing selfishness. But the politics of Cyrus were pervaded by purer motives, and this brought him eternal honour. The very same thing which the spirit of Darius, the father of Xerxes, is represented as saying of him in the <hi type="italic">Persae</hi> of Aeschylus (v. 735), Θεὸς γὰρ οὐκ ἤχθησεν ὡς εὔφρων ἔφυ (for he was not hateful to God, because he was well-disposed), is here said by the Spirit of revelation, which by no means regards the virtues of the heathen as <hi type="italic">splendida vitia</hi>. Jehovah has taken him by his right hand, to accomplish great things through him while supporting him thus. (On the inf. <hi type="italic">rad</hi> for <hi type="italic">rōd</hi>, from <hi type="italic">râdad</hi>, to tread down, see Ges. §67, Anm. 3.) The dual <hi type="italic">delâthaim</hi> has also a plural force: “double doors” (<hi type="italic">fores</hi>) in great number, viz., those of palaces. After the two infinitives, the verb passes into the finite tense: “loins of kings I ungird” (<hi type="italic">discingo</hi>; <hi type="italic">pittēăch</hi>, which refers primarily to the loosening of a fastened garment, is equivalent to depriving of strength). The gates - namely, those of the cities which he storms - will not be shut, sc. in perpetuity, that is to say, they will have to open to him. Jerome refers here to the account given of the elder Cyrus in Xenophon’s <hi type="italic">Cyropaedia</hi>. A general picture may no doubt be obtained from this of his success in war; but particular statements need support from other quarters, since it is only a historical romance. Instead of אושׁר (אושׁר)? in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Isa 45:2</reference>, the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> has אישּׁר; just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference> it has הישׁר instead of הושׁר. A <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> הושׁיר cannot really be shown to have existed, and the abbreviated future form עושׁר would be altogether without ground or object here. הדּורים (<hi type="italic">tumida</hi>; like נעיימם, <hi type="italic">amaena</hi>, and others) is meant to refer to the difficulties piled up in the conqueror’s way. The “<hi type="italic">gates of brass</hi>' (<hi type="italic">nedhūshâh</hi>, brazen, poetical for <hi type="italic">nechōsheth</hi>, brass, as in the derivative passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.16">Psa 107:16</reference>) and “<hi type="italic">bolts of iron</hi>” remind one more especially of Babylon with its hundred “brazen gates,” the very posts and lintels of which were also of brass (Herod. i. 179); and the <hi type="italic">treasures</hi> laid up in deep darkness and <hi type="italic">jewels</hi> preserved in hiding-places, of the riches of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jer 50:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jer 51:13</reference>), and especially of those of the Lydian Sardes, “the richest city of Asia after Babylon” (<hi type="italic">Cyrop.</hi> vii. 2, 11), which Cyrus conquered first. On the treasures which Cyrus acquired through his conquests, and to which allusion is made in the <hi type="italic">Persae</hi> of Aeschylus, v. 327 (“O Persian, land and harbour of many riches thou”), see Plin. <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> xxxiii. 2. Brerewood estimates the quantity of gold and silver mentioned there as captured by him at no less than £126,224,000 sterling. And all this success is given to him by Jehovah, that he may know that it is Jehovah the God of Israel who has called out with his name, i.e., called out his name, or called him to be what he is, and as what he shows himself to be.
entries.88afcdba364bcbd9da776aa26c053cc8edf78d5e: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4-Isa.45.7">Isa 45:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen13420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13421" type="x-p"/> A second and third object are introduced by a second and third למען. <hi type="italic">“For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I called thee hither by name, surnamed thee when thou knewest me not. I Jehovah, and there is none else, beside me no God: I equipped thee when thou knewest me not; that they may know from the rising of the sun, and its going down, that there is none without me: I Jehovah, and there is none else, former of the light, and creator of the darkness; founder of peace, and creator of evil: I Jehovah am He who worketh all this.”</hi> The ואקרא which follows the second reason assigned like an apodosis, is construed doubly: “I called to thee, calling thee by name.” The parallel אכנּך refers to such titles of honour as “my shepherd” and “my anointed,” which had been given to him by Jehovah. This calling, distinguishing, and girding, i.e., this equipment of Cyrus, took place at a time when Cyrus knew nothing as yet of Jehovah, and by this very fact Jehovah made known His sole Deity. The meaning is, not that it occurred while he was still worshipping false gods, but, as the <hi type="italic">refrain</hi>-like repetition of the words “though thou hast not know me” affirms with strong emphasis, before he had been brought into existence, or could know anything of Jehovah. The passage is to be explained in the same way as <reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jer 1:5</reference>, “Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee” (see <hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> pp. 36, 37, 39); and what the God of prophecy here claims for Himself, must not be questioned by false criticism, or weakened down by false apologetics (i.e., by giving up the proper name <hi type="italic">Cyrus</hi> as a gloss in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa 44:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">Isa 45:1</reference>; or generalizing it into a king’s name, such as Pharaoh, Abimelech, or Agag). The third and last object of this predicted and realized success of the oppressor of nations and deliverer of Israel is the acknowledgement of Jehovah, spreading over the heathen world from the rising and setting of the sun, i.e., in every direction. The <hi type="italic">ah</hi> of וּממּערבה is not a feminine termination (lxx, Targ., Jer.), but a feminine suffix with <hi type="italic">He</hi> <hi type="italic">raphato</hi> <hi type="italic">pro</hi> <hi type="italic">mappic</hi> (<hi type="italic">Kimchi</hi>); compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.17-Isa.23.18">Isa 23:17-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.17">Isa 34:17</reference> (but not נצּה in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.5">Isa 18:5</reference>, or מוּסדה in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Isa 30:32</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shemesh</hi> (the sun) is a feminine here, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen 15:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>, Mal 4:2, and always in Arabic; for the west is invariably called מערב (Arab. <hi type="italic">magrib</hi>). In <reference osisRef="Isa.45.7">Isa 45:7</reference> we are led by the context to understand by darkness and evil the penal judgments, through which light and peace, or salvation, break forth for the people of God and the nations generally. But as the prophecy concerning Cyrus closes with this self-assertion of Jehovah, it is unquestionably a natural supposition that there is also a contrast implied to the dualistic system of Zarathustra, which divided the one nature of the Deity into two opposing powers (see Windischmann, <hi type="italic">Zoroastrische Studien</hi>, p. 135). The declaration is so bold, that Marcion appealed to this passage as a proof that the God of the Old Testament was a different being from the God of the New, and not the God of goodness only. The Valentinians and other gnostics also regarded the words “There is no God beside me” in Isaiah, as deceptive words of the Demiurugs. The early church met them with Tertullian’s reply, <hi type="italic">“de his creator profitetur malis quae congruunt judici,”</hi> and also made use of this self-attestation of the God of revelation as a weapon with which to attack Manicheesism. The meaning of the words is not exhausted by those who content themselves with the assertion, that by the <hi type="italic">evil</hi> (or <hi type="italic">darkness</hi>) we are not to understand the evil of guilt (<hi type="italic">malum culpae</hi>), but the evil of punishment (<hi type="italic">malum paenae</hi>). Undoubtedly, evil as an act is not the direct working of God, but the spontaneous work of a creature endowed with freedom. At the same time, evil, as well as good, has in this sense its origin in God - that He combines within Himself the first principles of love and wrath, the possibility of evil, the self-punishment of evil, and therefore the consciousness of guilt as well as the evil of punishment in the broadest sense. When the apostle celebrates the glory of free grace in Rom 9:11., he stands on that giddy height, to which few are able to follow him without falling headlong into the false conclusions of a <hi type="italic">decretum absolutum</hi>, and the denial of all creaturely freedom.
entries.7512dccb1aab86e5973eb64586ab9d57050d8c38: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference> <div eID="gen13421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13422" type="x-p"/> In the prospect of this ultimate and saving purpose of the mission of Cyrus, viz., the redemption of Israel and the conversion of the heathen, heaven and earth are now summoned to bring forth and pour down spiritual blessings in heavenly gifts, according to the will and in the power of Jehovah, who has in view a new spiritual creation. <hi type="italic">“Cause to trickle down, ye heavens above, and let the blue sky rain down righteousness; let the earth open, and let salvation blossom, and righteousness; let them sprout together: I Jehovah have created it.”</hi> What the heavens are to cause to trickle down, follows as the object to יזּלוּ. And what is to flower when the earth opens (<hi type="italic">pâthach</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.17">Psa 106:17</reference>; compare <hi type="italic">aprilis</hi> and the Neo-Greek <hi type="italic">anoixis</hi>, spring), is salvation and righteousness. But <hi type="italic">tzedek</hi> (righteousness) is immediately afterwards the object of a new verb; so that וּצדקה ישׁע, which are thought of as combined, as the word יחד (together) shows, are uncoupled in the actual expression. Knobel expresses a different opinion, and assumes that ישׁע is regarded as a collective noun, and therefore construed with a plural, like אמרּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">Psa 119:103</reference>, and חמדה in Hag 2:7. But the use of <hi type="italic">yachad</hi> (together) favours the other interpretation. The suffix of בּראתיו points to this fulness of righteousness and salvation. It is a creation of Jehovah Himself. Heaven and earth, when co-operating to effect this, are endowed with their capacity through Him from whom cometh every good and perfect gift, and obey now, as at the first, His creative fiat. This <hi type="italic">“rorate caeli desuper et nubes pluant justum,”</hi> as the Vulgate renders it, is justly regarded as an old advent cry.
entries.9710ab08d56dbd02dcf90186fdd253bc428c9111: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9-Isa.45.10">Isa 45:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen13422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13423" type="x-p"/> The promise is now continued in the third strophe (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9-Isa.45.13">Isa 45:9-13</reference>), and increases more and more in the distinctness of its terms; but just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15-Isa.29.21">Isa 29:15-21</reference>, it opens with a reproof of that pusillanimity (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa 40:27</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Isa 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.24">Isa 49:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa 58:3</reference>), which goes so far to complain of the ways of Jehovah. <hi type="italic">“Woe to him that quarreleth with his Maker - a pot among the pots of earthenware? Can the clay indeed say to him that shapeth it, What makest thou? and thy work, He hath no hands? Woe to him that saith to his father, What begettest thou? and to the woman, What bringest thou forth?”</hi> The comparison drawn between a man as the work of God and the clay-work of a potter suggested itself all the more naturally, inasmuch as the same word yootseer was applied to God as Creator, and also to a potter (<hi type="italic">figulus</hi>). The word <hi type="italic">cheres</hi> signifies either a sherd, or fragment of earthenware (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.14">Isa 30:14</reference>), or an earthenware vessel (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.1">Jer 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Pro 26:23</reference>). In the passage before us, where the point of comparison is not the fragmentary condition, but the earthen character of the material ()<hi type="italic">'adâmâh</hi>), the latter is intended: the man, who complains of God, is nothing but a vessel of clay, and, more than that, a perishable vessel among many others of the very same kind.<note placement="foot">The Septuagint reads <hi type="italic">shin</hi> for <hi type="italic">sin</hi> in both instances, and introduces here the very unsuitable thought already contained in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.24">Isa 28:24</reference>, “Shall the ploughman plough the land the whole day?”</note> <div eID="gen13423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13424" type="x-p"/> The questions which follow are meant to show the folly of this complaining. Can it possibly occur to the clay to raise a complaint against him who has it in hand, that he has formed it in such and such a manner, or for such and such a purpose (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Rom 9:20</reference>, “Why hast thou made me thus”)? To the words “or thy work” we must supply <hi type="italic">num dicet</hi> (shall it say); <hi type="italic">pō‛al</hi> is a manufacture, as in Isa 1:31. The question is addressed to the maker, as those in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.25">Isa 7:25</reference> are to the husbandman: Can the thing made by thee, O man, possibly say in a contemptuous tone, “He has no hands?” - a supposition the ridiculous absurdity of which condemns it at once; and yet it is a very suitable analogy to the conduct of the man who complains of God. In <reference osisRef="Isa.45.10">Isa 45:10</reference> a woe is denounced upon those who resemble a man who should say to his own father, What children dost thou beget? or to a wife, What dost thou bring forth? (<hi type="italic">techı̄lı̄n</hi> an emphatic, and for the most part pausal, <hi type="italic">fut. parag.</hi>, as in Rth 2:8; Rth 3:18). This would be the rudest and most revolting attack upon an inviolably tender and private relation; and yet Israel does this when it makes the hidden providential government of its God the object of expostulation.
entries.26c3c6df7fcfa83a86a424bde95f56a8222b3658: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.11-Isa.45.12">Isa 45:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen13424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> After this double woe, which is expressed in general terms, but the application of which is easily made, the words of Jehovah are directly addressed to the presumptuous criticizers. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.11">Isa 45:11</reference> <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah, the Holy One of Israel, and its Maker, Ask me what is to come; let my sons and the work of my hands be committed to me!”</hi> The names by which He calls Himself express his absolute blamelessness, and His absolute right of supremacy over Israel. שׁאלוּני is an imperative, like שׁמעוּני in <reference osisRef="Gen.23.8">Gen 23:8</reference>; the third person would be written שׁאלוּני. The meaning is: If ye would have any information or satisfaction concerning the future (“things to come,” <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">Isa 41:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Isa 44:7</reference>), about which ye can neither know nor determine anything of yourselves, inquire of me. צוּה with an accusative of the person, and על of the thing, signifies to commit anything to the care of another (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.12">1Ch 22:12</reference>). The fault-finders in Israel were to leave the people of whom Jehovah was the Maker (a retrospective allusion to <reference osisRef="Isa.45.10">Isa 45:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa 45:9</reference>), in the hands of Him who has created everything, and on whom everything depends. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.12">Isa 45:12</reference> <hi type="italic">“I, I have made the earth, and created men upon it; I, my hands have stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I called forth.”</hi> ידי אני, according to Ges. §121, 3, is equivalent to my hands, and mine alone - a similar arrangement of words to those in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.27">Gen 24:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.10">2Ch 28:10</reference>; Ecc 2:15. Hitzig is wrong in his rendering, “all their host do I command.” That of Ewald is the correct one, “did I appoint;” for <hi type="italic">tsivvâsh</hi>, followed by an accusative of the person, means to give a definite order or command to any one, the command in this case being the order to come into actual existence (= <hi type="italic">esse jussi</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">Psa 33:9</reference>).
entries.d8f3ec737504e01554a3cc2eb5ac71fb88c6dc0a: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.13">Isa 45:13</reference> <div eID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> He who created all things, and called all things into existence, had also raised up this Cyrus, whose victorious career had increased the anxieties and fears of the exiles, instead of leading them to lift up their heads, because their redemption was drawing nigh. <hi type="italic">“I, I have raised him up in righteousness, and all his ways shall I make smooth: He will build my city, and release my banished ones, not for price nor for reward, saith Jehovah of hosts.”</hi> All the anxieties of the exiles are calmed by the words “in righteousness,” which trace back the revolutions that Cyrus was causing to the righteousness of Jehovah, i.e., to His interposition, which was determined by love alone, and tended directly to the salvation of His people, and in reality to that of all nations. And they are fully quieted by the promise, which is now expressed in the clearest and most unequivocal words, that Cyrus would build up Jerusalem again, and set the captivity free (<hi type="italic">gâlūth</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.20.4">Isa 20:4</reference>), and that without redemption with money (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.3">Isa 52:3</reference>) - a clear proof that Jehovah had not only raised up Cyrus himself, but had put his spirit within him, i.e., had stirred up within him the resolution to do this (see the conclusion to the books of Chronicles, and the introduction to that of Ezra). This closes the first half of our sixth prophecy.
entries.375cc0eceba108ec3556d26885bb019bbe0f1d76: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference> <div eID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> The second half is uttered in the prospect, that the judgment which Cyrus brings upon the nations will prepare the way for the overthrow of heathenism, and the universal acknowledgment of the God of Israel. The heathen submit, as the first strophe or group of vv. (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.14-Isa.45.17">Isa 45:14-17</reference>) affirms, to the congregation and its God; the idolatrous are converted, whilst Israel is for ever redeemed. With the prospect of the release of the exiles, there is associated in the prophet’s perspective the prospect of an expansion of the restored church, through the entrance of “the fulness of the Gentiles.” <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah, The productions of Egypt, and gain of Ethiopia, and the Sabaeans, men of tall stature, will come over to thee, and belong to thee: they will come after thee; in chains they will come over, and cast themselves down to thee; they pray to thee, Surely God is in thee, and there is none else; no Deity at all.”</hi> Assuming that יעברוּ has the same meaning in both cases, the prophet’s meaning appears to be, that the Egyptians, Ethiopians, and Meroites (see <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3">Isa 43:3</reference>), who had been enslaved by the imperial power of Persia, would enter the miraculously emancipated congregation of Israel (Ewald). But if they were thought of as in a state of subjugation to the imperial power of Asia, who could the promise be at the same time held out that their riches would pass over into the possession of the church? And yet, on the other hand, the chains in which they come over cannot be regarded, at least in this connection, where such emphasis is laid upon the voluntary character of the surrender, as placed upon them by Israel itself (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.11">Isa 60:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.149.8">Psa 149:8</reference>). We must therefore suppose that they put chains upon themselves voluntarily, and of their own accord, and thus offer themselves spontaneously to the church, to be henceforth its subjects and slaves. Egypt, Ethiopia, and Saba are the nations that we meet with in other passages, where the <hi type="italic">haereditas gentium</hi> is promised to the church, and generally in connection with Tyre (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.68.32">Psa 68:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">Psa 72:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference>; Isa 19:16., <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa 23:18</reference>). Whilst the labour of Egypt (i.e., the productions of its labour) and the trade of Ethiopia (i.e., the riches acquired by trade) are mentioned; in the case of Saba the prophecy looks at the tall and handsome tribe itself, a tribe which Agatharchides describes as having σώματα ἀξιολογώτερα. These would place themselves at the service of the church with their invincible strength. The voluntary character of the surrender is pointed out, not only in the expression “they will come over,” but also in the confession with which this is accompanied. In other cases the words <hi type="italic">hithpallēl 'el</hi> are only used of prayer to God and idols; but here it is to the church that prayer is offered. In the prophet’s view, Jehovah and His church are inseparably one (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">1Co 12:12</reference>, where “Christ” stands for the church as one body, consisting of both head and members; also the use of the word “worship” in <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev 3:9</reference>, which has all the ring of a passage taken from Isaiah). אך is used here in its primary affirmative sense, as in Psa 58:11. There can be no doubt that Paul had this passage of Isaiah in his mind when writing <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24-1Cor.14.25">1Co 14:24-25</reference>, ἀπαγγέλλων ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς ὄντως ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστί, or, according to a better arrangement of the words, ὅτι ὄντως (= אך) ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστίν. <hi type="italic">'Ephes</hi> does not signify <hi type="italic">praeter</hi> (as a synonym of בּלעדי, זוּלתי) either here or anywhere else, but is a substantive used with a verbal force, which stands in the same relation to אין as “there is not at all (absolutely not)” to “there is not;” compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.6">Isa 45:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.9">Isa 46:9</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference> (derivative passage, 2Ki 14:26), and <reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">Amo 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.3">2Sa 9:3</reference>; vid., Isa 47:8.
entries.02f63b8465512fc899c486fa8b02d18ac2836df3: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa 45:15</reference> <div eID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> What follows in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa 45:15</reference> is not a continuation of the words of the Gentiles, but a response of the church to their confession. The nations that have been idolatrous till now, bend in humble spontaneous worship before the church and its God; and at the sight of this, the church, from whose soul the prophet is speaking, bursts out into an exclamation of reverential amazement. <hi type="italic">“Verily Thou art a mysterious God, Thou God of Israel, Thou Savour.”</hi> Literally, a God who hides Himself (<hi type="italic">mistattēr</hi>: the resemblance to μυστηρ-ιώδης is quite an accidental one; the <hi type="italic">ē</hi> is retained in the participle even in pause). The meaning is, a God who guides with marvellous strangeness the history of the nations of the earth, and by secret ways, which human eyes can never discern, conducts all to a glorious issue. The exclamation in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom 11:33</reference>, “O the depth of the riches,” etc., is a similar one.
entries.6bb2e914197dfc3a73ace5157623b6cfc1d76acc: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.16-Isa.45.17">Isa 45:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> The way in which this God who hides Himself is ultimately revealed as the God of salvation, is then pointed out in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Isa 45:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.17">Isa 45:17</reference> : <hi type="italic">“They are put to shame, and also confounded, all of them; they go away into confusion together, the forgers of idols. Israel is redeemed by Jehovah with everlasting redemption: ye are not put to shame nor confounded to everlasting eternities.”</hi> The perfects are expressive of the ideal past. Jehovah shows Himself as a Savour by the fact, that whereas the makers of idols perish, Israel is redeemed an everlasting redemption (acc. obj. as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">Isa 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.17">Isa 22:17</reference>; Ges. §138, 1, Anm. 1), i.e., so that its redemption is one that lasts for aeons (αἰωνία λύτρωσις, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb 9:12</reference>) - observe that <hi type="italic">teshū‛âh</hi> does not literally signify redemption or rescue, but transfer into a state of wide expanse, i.e., of freedom and happiness. The plural <hi type="italic">‛ōlâmı̄m</hi> (eternities = αἰῶνες <hi type="italic">aeua</hi>) belongs, according to Knobel, to the later period of the language; but it is met with as early as in old Asaphite psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.6">Psa 77:6</reference>). When the further promise is added, Ye shall not be put to shame, etc., this clearly shows, what is also certain on other grounds - namely, that the redemption is not thought of merely as an outward and bodily one, but also as inward and spiritual, and indeed (in accordance with the prophetic blending of the end of the captivity with the end of all things) as a final one. Israel will never bring upon itself again such a penal judgment as that of the captivity by falling away from God; that is to say, its state of sin will end with its state of punishment, even עב עד־עולמי, i.e., since עד has no plural, εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων.
entries.e5da162af385fc5c875b5d507dc3b9d03f001f0c: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.18-Isa.45.19">Isa 45:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> The second and last strophe of this prophecy commences with Isa 45:18. By the fulfilment of the promise thus openly proclaimed, those of the heathen who have been saved from the judgment will recognise Jehovah as the only God; and the irresistible will of Jehovah, that all mankind should worship Him, be carried out. The promise cannot remain unfulfilled. <hi type="italic">“For thus saith Jehovah, the creator of the heavens </hi>(<hi type="italic">He is the Deity</hi>)<hi type="italic">, the former of the earth, and its finisher; He has established it </hi>(<hi type="italic">He has not created it a desert, He has formed it to be inhabited</hi>)<hi type="italic">: I am Jehovah, and there is none else. I have not spoken in secret, in a place of the land of darkness; I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Into the desert seek ye me! I Jehovah am speaking righteousness, proclaiming upright things.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">athnach</hi> properly divides <reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa 45:18</reference> in half. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa 45:18</reference></hi> describes the speaker, and what He says commences in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa 45:18</reference></hi>. The first parenthesis affirms that Jehovah is God in the fullest and most exclusive sense; the second that He has created the earth for man’s sake, not “as a desert” (<hi type="italic">tōhū</hi>: the lxx, Targum, and Jerome render this with less accuracy, <hi type="italic">non in vanum</hi>), i.e., not to be and continue to be a desert, but to be inhabited. Even in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>, <hi type="italic">chaos</hi> is not described as of God’s creation, because (whatever may be men’s opinions concerning it in other respects) the creative activity of God merely made use of this as a starting-point, and because, although it did not come into existence without God, it was at any rate not desired by God for its own sake. The words of Jehovah commence, then, with the assertion that Jehovah is the absolute One; and from this two thoughts branch off: (1.) The first is, that the prophecy which emanates from Him is an affair of light, no black art, but essentially different from heathen soothsaying. By “a dark place of the earth” we are to understand, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>, the interior of the earth, and according to <reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job 10:21</reference>, Hades; the intention being to point out the contrast between the prophecies of Jehovah and the heathen cave-oracles and spirit-voices of the necromancists, which seemed to rise up from the interior of the earth (see <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Isa 65:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Isa 29:4</reference>). (2.) The second thought is, that the very same love of Jehovah, which has already been displayed in the creation, attests itself in His relation to Israel, which He has not directed to Himself “into the desert” (<hi type="italic">tōhū</hi>), just as He did not create the earth a <hi type="italic">tōhū</hi>. Meier and Knobel suppose that <hi type="italic">baqshūnı̄</hi>, which is written here, according to a well-supported reading, with <hi type="italic">Koph</hi> <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi> (whereas in other cases the <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> is generally retained, particularly in the imperative of <hi type="italic">biqqēsh</hi>), refers to seeking for disclosures as to the future; but the word דרשׁוּני would be used for this, as in Isa 8:19. He has not said, “Seek ye me (as in Zep 2:3) into the desert,” i.e., without the prospect of meeting with any return for your pains. On the contrary, He has attached promises to the seeking of Himself, which cannot remain unfulfilled, for He is “one speaking righteousness, declaring things that are right;” i.e., when He promises, He follows out the rule of His purpose and of His plan of salvation, and the impulse of sincere desire for their good, and love which is ever true to itself. The present word of prophecy points to the fulfilment of these promises.
entries.3375b793e55cfdeebe0127e2c905a4721f200189: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.20-Isa.45.21">Isa 45:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> The salvation of Israel, foretold and realized by Jehovah, becomes at the same time the salvation of the heathen world. <hi type="italic">“Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, ye escaped of the heathen! Irrational are they who burden themselves with the wood of their idol, and pray to a god that bringeth no salvation. Make known, and cause to draw near; yea, let them take counsel together: Who has made such things known from the olden time, proclaimed it long ago? have not I, Jehovah? and there is no Deity beside me; a God just, and bringing salvation: there is not without me!”</hi> The fulness of the Gentiles, which enters into the kingdom of God, is a remnant of the whole mass of the heathen: for salvation comes through judgment; and it is in the midst of great calamities that the work of that heathen mission is accomplished, which is represented in these prophecies on the one hand as the mission of Cyrus, and on the other hand as the mission of Jehovah and His servant. Hence this summons to listen to the self-assertion of the God of revelation, is addressed to the escaped of the heathen, who are not therefore the converted, but those who are susceptible of salvation, and therefore spared. By “the heathen” (<hi type="italic">haggōyı̄m</hi>) Knobel understands the allies and auxiliaries of the Babylonians, whom Cyrus put to flight (according to the <hi type="italic">Cyropaedia</hi>) before his Lydian campaign. But this is only an example of that exaggerated desire to turn everything into history, which not only prevented his seeing the poetry of the form, but obscured the fact that prophecy is both human and divine. For the future was foreshortened to the telescopic glance of the prophet, so that he could not see it in all its length and breadth. He saw in one mass what history afterwards unrolled; and then behind the present he could just see as it were the summit of the end, although a long eventful way still lay between the two. Accordingly, our prophet here takes his stand not at the close of any particular victory of Cyrus, but at the close of all his victories; and, in his view, these terminate the whole series of catastrophes, which are outlived by a remnant of the heathen, who are converted to Jehovah, and thus complete the final glory of the restored people of God. Throughout the whole of these prophecies we see immediately behind the historical foreground this eschatological background lifting up its head. The heathen who have been preserved will assemble together; and from the fact that Jehovah proves Himself the sole foreteller of the events that are now unfolding themselves, they will be brought to the conviction that He is the only God. The <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> <hi type="italic">hithnaggēsh</hi> does not occur anywhere else. On the absolute ידע לא, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>). To the verb <hi type="italic">haggı̄shū</hi> we must supply, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.22">Isa 41:22</reference>, according to the same expression in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Isa 45:21</reference>, עצּמתיכם (your proofs). “<hi type="italic">This</hi>” refers to the fall of Babylon and redemption of Israel - salvation breaking through judgment. On <hi type="italic">mē'âz</hi>, from the olden time, compare Isa 44:8. God is “a just God and a Saviour,” as a being who acts most stringently according to the demands of His holiness, and wherever His wrath is not wickedly provoked, sets in motion His loving will, which is ever concerned to secure the salvation of men.
entries.b39f71c5f2845622a1b2ea55daeb5cca577f7792: <reference osisRef="Isa.45.22-Isa.45.23">Isa 45:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> It is in accordance with this holy loving will that the cry is published in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Isa 45:22</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Turn unto me, and be ye saved, all ye ends of the earth; for I am God, and none else.”</hi> The first imperative is hortatory, the second promising (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.36.16">Isa 36:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>): Jehovah desires both, viz., the conversion of all men to Himself; and through this their salvation, ad this His gracious will, which extends to all mankind, will not rest till its object has been fully accomplished. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Isa 45:23</reference> <hi type="italic">“By myself have I sworn, a word has gone out of a mouth of righteousness, and will not return, That to me every knee shall bend, every tongue swear.”</hi> Swearing by Himself (see <reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Gen 22:16</reference>), God pledges what He swears with His own life (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Rom 14:11</reference>, “as I live”). Parallel to נשׁבּעתּי בּי is the clause ישׁוּב ולא דּבר צדק מפּי יצא. Here Rosenmüller connects דבר צדקה together as if with a hyphen, in the sense of a truth-word (Jerome, <hi type="italic">justitiae verbum</hi>). But this is grammatically impossible, since it would require צדקה דּבר; moreover, it is opposed both to the accents, and to the <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Daleth</hi>. Hitzig’s rendering is a better one: “Truth (lxx δικαιοσύνη), a word that does not return,” - the latter being taken as an explanatory permutative; but in that case we should require לא for ולא, and <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi> is not used in the sense of truth anywhere else (compare <hi type="italic">tsaddı̄q</hi>, however, in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Isa 41:26</reference>). On the other hand, צדקה might be equivalent to בצדקה “in righteousness;” cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>, חמה = בּהמה), if it were not incomparably more natural to connect together צדקה מפי as a genitive construction; though not in the sense in which הגבורה מפי is used in post-biblical writings - namely, as equivalent to “out of the mouth of God” (see Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Lex. Chald.</hi> Col. 385) - ) - but rather in this way, that the mouth of God is described attributively as regulated in its words by His holy will (as “speaking righteousness, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa 45:19</reference></hi>). A word has gone forth from this mouth of righteousness; and after it has once gone forth, it does not return without accomplishing its object (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Isa 55:11</reference>). What follows is not so much a promising prediction (that every knee will bend to me), as a definitive declaration of will (that it shall or must bend to me). According to <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Isa 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference>, “to me” is to be regarded as carried forward, and so to be supplied after “shall swear” (the Septuagint rendering, ὀμεῖται … τὸν Θεόν, is false; that of Paul in <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Rom 14:11</reference>, ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ Θεῷ, is correct; and in this case, as in others also, the <hi type="italic">Cod. Al.</hi> of the Sept. has been corrected from the New Testament quotations).
